canonical_statement: The study aimed to compare time to target anti-Xa and evidence of major bleeding between obese and nonobese patients treated with the same adjusted-body-weight-based UFH infusion protocol.
This was a single-center retrospective cohort study at a 620-bed academic medical center using patients initiated on IV UFH for VTE from January 1, 2018 through December 31, 2023.
Eligible patients were at least 18 years old and received IV UFH for treatment of VTE for at least 24 hours.

population.label: Eligible study population
inclusion_criteria: IV UFH for treatment of VTE for at least 24 hours

canonical_statement: Patients were excluded for prior anticoagulant use before admission or UFH treatment, thrombolytic use before or during UFH, UFH initiation at another institution, non-AdjBW UFH dosing, pregnancy, or incarceration.

population.label: Excluded patients
exclusion_criteria: Anticoagulant use prior to admission or prior to UFH treatment
Thrombolytic administered prior to or during UFH treatment
Adjusted body weight not used for UFH dosing

canonical_statement: The institution used adjusted body weight for all protocol UFH dosing except when total body weight was less than adjusted body weight; boluses and maintenance infusions had no dose caps.

exposures.details: Use TBW instead when TBW < AdjBW; no bolus or infusion dose caps.

canonical_statement: The institutional protocol recommended an optional 80 units/kg initial UFH bolus followed by an initial infusion of 18 units/kg/hour.
Anti-Xa levels were collected every 6 hours with nurse-driven UFH dose adjustments targeting an anti-Xa range of 0.3 to 0.7 IU/mL.
For anti-Xa values below 0.15 IU/mL, the protocol called for an 80 units/kg bolus, an infusion increase of 4 units/kg/hour, and repeat anti-Xa testing in 6 hours.
For anti-Xa values of 0.15 to 0.29 IU/mL, the protocol called for a 40 units/kg bolus, an infusion increase of 2 units/kg/hour, and repeat anti-Xa testing in 6 hours.
For anti-Xa values of 0.3 to 0.7 IU/mL, the protocol specified no dose adjustment and repeat anti-Xa testing the next morning.
For anti-Xa values of 0.71 to 1.0 IU/mL, the protocol specified decreasing the infusion by 2 units/kg/hour and repeating anti-Xa testing in 6 hours.
For anti-Xa values above 1.0 IU/mL, the protocol specified holding the infusion for 1 hour, then decreasing it by 3 units/kg/hour, with repeat anti-Xa testing in 6 hours.
The primary outcome was median time from UFH infusion initiation to the first target anti-Xa value, with target defined as 0.3 to 0.7 IU/mL.

outcome.definition: Hours from UFH infusion start to first anti-Xa value within 0.3-0.7 IU/mL

canonical_statement: A secondary outcome was time to the second consecutive anti-Xa value within the target range.

outcome.definition: Time to the second consecutive anti-Xa value within 0.3-0.7 IU/mL

canonical_statement: Secondary analyses categorized the first anti-Xa value at 6 hours as within, above, or below the 0.3 to 0.7 IU/mL target range.

outcome.definition: First anti-Xa after UFH initiation categorized as within, above, or below the 0.3-0.7 IU/mL target range

canonical_statement: Evidence of major bleeding was defined as bleeding causing a hemoglobin decrease of at least 2 g/dL or leading to transfusion of at least 2 units of packed red blood cells.

outcome.definition: Bleeding causing a hemoglobin fall of at least 2 g/dL or transfusion of at least 2 units of packed red blood cells
outcome.measurement_method: ISTH major bleeding criteria as operationalized by the study

canonical_statement: Obesity was defined as BMI at least 30 kg/m2; class 1 was BMI 30.0-34.9, class 2 was 35.0-39.9, and class 3 was at least 40.0 kg/m2.

Continuous outcomes were analyzed with Mann-Whitney U tests, categorical outcomes with chi-square or Fisher exact tests, obese subgroup continuous outcomes with Kruskal-Wallis tests, and subgroup categorical outcomes with chi-square tests of independence; alpha was 0.05.
The analyzed cohort included 166 patients: 75 obese and 91 nonobese.

canonical_statement: Among the 14 patients meeting the study major-bleed definition, 13 met the hemoglobin-decrease criterion and 1 met the transfusion criterion; no patient had UFH therapy interrupted because of the event.
The authors reported no deviations from nurse-driven dose adjustments; protocol adjustments required dual nursing sign-off and pharmacist verification.

The recommended initial infusion rate of 18 units/kg/hour was used in 148 of 166 patients (89.16%); 18 patients (10.84%) started at another rate, with no statistically significant difference in this distribution by obesity group (P=0.15).

canonical_statement: The authors identified the small sample size and retrospective design as study limitations.
The single academic medical center and limited population diversity may reduce generalizability to other institutions.
Because of the retrospective design, potentially mistimed anti-Xa laboratory values could not be fully accounted for.
The initial 80 units/kg bolus and 18 units/kg/hour infusion were protocol suggestions rather than requirements, and 10.84% of patients started at a rate other than 18 units/kg/hour.
The study did not report total heparin dose in units/hour when target anti-Xa was achieved, limiting extrapolation to centers using TBW and/or dose caps.
The authors cautioned that findings based on anti-Xa-guided dose adjustment may not extrapolate appropriately to institutions using aPTT monitoring.
The authors noted that the observed major-bleed frequency may be affected by the absence of a specified time frame for the hemoglobin decrease criterion used to operationalize major bleeding.

The authors concluded that obese and nonobese patients had no observed difference in median time to first target anti-Xa or evidence of major bleeding when treated with the adjusted-body-weight UFH protocol.
The authors stated that their findings support a simplified approach using adjusted body weight for UFH dosing in both obese and nonobese patients when anti-Xa is used for monitoring.
